youtube.title: Why Do We Need Leap Years? (And the 11 Days Britain Lost)
youtube.description:
In September 1752, Britain went to bed on the 2nd and woke up on the 14th. Eleven days vanished by law, all because a year isn't really 365 days.

From Julius Caesar's 445-day 'year of confusion' and Pope Gregory's deleted days in 1582, to why 1900 had no February 29th but 2000 did, and why the October Revolution happened in November: this is the hidden why behind the leap year.

instagram.caption:
In 1752, Britain skipped from September 2nd straight to September 14th. 📅

A year is really 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes. Caesar's leap year overshot by 11 minutes a year, and 16 centuries later the calendar was 10 days off. The fix: century years skip the leap day, unless they divide by 400.

Full story on our YouTube channel.

facts: Tropical year ~365.2422 days = 365 d 5 h 48-49 min (RMG, Britannica)
46 BC: Julian calendar, Sosigenes; 46 BC lasted 445 days, 'year of confusion' (Britannica Julian calendar)
Julian year 365.25 d is ~11 min too long; ~10 days drift by 1582 (Britannica Gregorian)
1582: Thu 4 Oct followed by Fri 15 Oct; century rule /400 (Britannica Gregorian, RMG)
Britain: Calendar Act 1750, 2 Sep 1752 followed by 14 Sep (UK Parliament)
'Give us our eleven days' riots: little or no evidence (RMG, historians)
Russia adopted Gregorian in 1918; Oct 25 1917 Julian = Nov 7 Gregorian (Britannica)
Gregorian year 365.2425 d vs 365.2422: ~27 s/yr, ~1 day per ~3,000+ years
No leap years: 0.2422 d/yr drift, ~182 days (half a year) in ~750 years
